title: Mental Health — Mania & Lithium II: Safety, Toxicity Risk & Application (Set 24)
subtitle: Phase-2 depth: prioritizing acute mania (exhaustion, dehydration, impulsivity, injury), recognizing lithium toxicity as an emergency and holding/reporting, applying the situations that raise toxicity risk (dehydration, sodium/fluid loss, NSAIDs, diuretics, heat/exertion), sick-day and consistent-salt teaching, adherence and nonjudgmental support, and the technician's monitoring/reporting role
scenario: Keeping the manic client safe and the client on lithium out of danger: spotting exhaustion and dehydration before collapse, recognizing toxicity early and holding the dose, applying what raises lithium levels, and supporting adherence without judgment.

steps.q: A client in acute mania has not slept or eaten for two days, is soaked with sweat, and keeps pacing. Which is the SAFETY priority?

opts.text: Physical exhaustion and dehydration—address rest, fluids, and nutrition, because the client can collapse
opts.rat: Sustained hyperactivity without sleep, food, or fluids can lead to exhaustion, dehydration, and physical collapse, making physical safety the priority.

opts.text: Whether the client's plans are realistic
opts.rat: Debating the realism of manic plans is not the physical-safety priority.

opts.text: Getting the client to sit quietly for a long group
opts.rat: A long, demanding activity is not appropriate and is not the priority for an exhausted, dehydrated client.

opts.text: Correcting the client's grammar and speech
opts.rat: This is irrelevant to the client's physical safety.

steps.q: Because a manic client cannot sit still to eat, the BEST way to support nutrition and hydration is to:

opts.text: Offer high-calorie finger foods and fluids the client can carry while moving
opts.rat: Portable finger foods and drinks let the restless client take in calories and fluids without having to sit for a full meal.

opts.text: Insist the client sit for a full plated meal or eat nothing
opts.rat: A manic client often cannot sit for a full meal; insisting risks the client eating nothing.

opts.text: Withhold food until the client calms down
opts.rat: Withholding food from an already-depleted client is unsafe.

opts.text: Provide only foods that require utensils and a table
opts.rat: Utensil-and-table foods are hard for a client who cannot stay seated.

steps.q: The most appropriate environment for a client in acute mania is:

opts.text: Calm, low-stimulation, and structured, with routines and space to move safely
opts.rat: Reducing stimulation while providing structure and safe outlets for energy helps limit escalation and protects the manic client.

opts.text: Busy and highly stimulating to match the client's energy
opts.rat: High stimulation tends to worsen manic hyperactivity.

opts.text: A large, competitive group activity
opts.rat: Competitive, crowded activities can overstimulate and escalate the client.

opts.text: Complete isolation in a dark locked room
opts.rat: Isolation/seclusion is not a routine environment and is not indicated simply for mania.

steps.q: A client on maintenance lithium develops a coarse hand tremor, slurred speech, an unsteady gait, vomiting, and new confusion. The technician should:

opts.text: Recognize possible lithium toxicity, hold the next dose, and report to the nurse immediately
opts.rat: These are classic signs of lithium toxicity—a medical emergency; the dose is held and the nurse is notified at once.

opts.text: Give the next dose early to steady the tremor
opts.rat: Giving more lithium when toxicity is suspected is dangerous.

opts.text: Assume it is normal and document only
opts.rat: These findings are not normal; they require holding the dose and prompt reporting.

opts.text: Encourage the client to keep taking lithium as scheduled without telling anyone
opts.rat: Continuing the dose without reporting suspected toxicity is unsafe.

steps.q: Which client on lithium is the technician's priority to assess FIRST?

opts.text: A client who has had vomiting and diarrhea all day and now feels dizzy and shaky
opts.rat: Fluid loss and dehydration raise lithium levels and can precipitate toxicity, so this client is assessed first.

opts.text: A client asking when the next group session starts
opts.rat: A routine question is not a priority over possible toxicity.

opts.text: A client who wants a second helping at lunch
opts.rat: A meal request is not a safety priority.

opts.text: A client requesting to call a family member
opts.rat: A phone-call request is not an urgent safety concern.

steps.q: A client on lithium develops a stomach virus with vomiting and diarrhea. The technician should apply which 'sick-day' principle?

opts.text: Illness with fluid loss can raise lithium to a dangerous level, so report it promptly and follow orders about the dose
opts.rat: Vomiting, diarrhea, and reduced intake concentrate lithium and raise the level; the situation is reported and managed per orders, not ignored.

opts.text: Nothing changes; keep giving lithium and fluids as usual and do not report it
opts.rat: Fluid loss can push lithium into the toxic range, so it must be reported.

opts.text: Double the lithium dose to make up for vomiting
opts.rat: Doubling the dose is unsafe and outside scope.

opts.text: Restrict all fluids until the vomiting stops
opts.rat: Fluid restriction worsens dehydration and toxicity risk.

steps.q: A client on lithium plans to start intense outdoor exercise during hot summer weather. The technician's teaching should emphasize that:

opts.text: Heavy sweating and dehydration can raise lithium levels, so the client should maintain fluids and report symptoms of toxicity
opts.rat: Excessive sweating and dehydration from heat and exertion can raise lithium levels, so adequate fluid intake and symptom awareness are important.

opts.text: Sweating lowers lithium, so extra exercise is a good way to reduce the dose
opts.rat: Sweating and dehydration raise, not lower, lithium levels.

opts.text: Fluid intake has no effect on lithium
opts.rat: Fluid balance strongly affects lithium levels.

opts.text: The client should avoid all fluids while exercising
opts.rat: Avoiding fluids during exertion is dangerous and raises toxicity risk.

steps.q: A client on lithium says, 'I've decided to cut way back on salt to eat healthier.' The technician recognizes that a sudden drop in dietary sodium can:

opts.text: Raise the lithium level and increase toxicity risk, so the change should be reported to the team
opts.rat: Lower sodium intake causes the body to retain more lithium, raising the level; a marked change in salt intake is reported so the team can respond.

opts.text: Have no effect on lithium at all
opts.rat: Sodium intake meaningfully affects lithium levels.

opts.text: Always lower the lithium level safely
opts.rat: Reduced sodium tends to raise, not safely lower, lithium levels.

opts.text: Be encouraged without informing anyone
opts.rat: A significant sodium change should be communicated because it affects lithium levels.

steps.q: A client on lithium asks to take an over-the-counter medication for a headache. Which class should the technician flag to the nurse because it can raise lithium levels?

opts.text: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen
opts.rat: NSAIDs can reduce lithium excretion and raise lithium levels, so their use should be cleared with the team.

opts.text: Plain acetaminophen only
opts.rat: Acetaminophen is generally the safer choice and is not the class known to raise lithium the way NSAIDs do.

opts.text: Throat lozenges
opts.rat: Lozenges are not the concern for raising lithium levels.

opts.text: Saline nasal spray
opts.rat: Saline spray does not raise lithium levels.

steps.q: A client on lithium is newly started on a diuretic ('water pill') by another provider. The technician should:

opts.text: Report the new medication, because diuretics can change fluid and sodium balance and affect lithium levels
opts.rat: Diuretics alter sodium and fluid balance and can raise lithium levels, so the change is reported to the team for monitoring.

opts.text: Ignore it, since other providers' medications never interact with lithium
opts.rat: Medications like diuretics can significantly affect lithium levels.

opts.text: Tell the client to stop the lithium instead
opts.rat: Stopping lithium is outside scope; the interaction is reported to licensed staff.

opts.text: Advise the client to drink far less water to balance it out
opts.rat: Reducing fluids can worsen toxicity risk; management belongs to the team.

steps.q: Which early symptom should the technician teach a client on lithium to report right away?

opts.text: New nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hand tremor, or muscle weakness
opts.rat: These early signs can indicate a rising lithium level and should be reported promptly before toxicity worsens.

opts.text: Feeling calm and sleeping normally
opts.rat: Calm mood and normal sleep are reassuring, not warning signs.

opts.text: A mild improvement in appetite
opts.rat: Improved appetite is not a toxicity warning sign.

opts.text: Enjoying a social activity
opts.rat: Normal engagement is not a symptom to report.

steps.q: Because lithium has a narrow margin between a helpful and a harmful level, the client should be taught to:

opts.text: Take it consistently as prescribed, keep lab-monitoring appointments, and maintain steady fluid and salt intake
opts.rat: Consistent dosing, regular blood-level monitoring, and steady fluid/sodium intake keep lithium in a safe, effective range.

opts.text: Adjust the dose on their own based on how they feel that day
opts.rat: Self-adjusting a narrow-range drug is dangerous; dosing is set by the prescriber.

opts.text: Skip blood tests once they feel stable
opts.rat: Ongoing monitoring stays necessary even when the client feels well.

opts.text: Vary fluid and salt intake widely from day to day
opts.rat: Wide swings in fluid or salt destabilize lithium levels.

steps.q: A client stops taking lithium, saying, 'I missed the high energy and the way I felt on top of the world.' The MOST therapeutic response is to:

opts.text: Explore this nonjudgmentally, acknowledge the appeal of the manic 'high,' and report the nonadherence to the team
opts.rat: Missing the manic high is a common reason clients stop mood stabilizers; a nonjudgmental approach plus reporting supports safe re-engagement in treatment.

opts.text: Scold the client for being irresponsible
opts.rat: Scolding is nontherapeutic and discourages honesty.

opts.text: Agree that stopping the medication is a good idea
opts.rat: Encouraging nonadherence is unsafe and outside scope.

opts.text: Say nothing to the team about the missed doses
opts.rat: Nonadherence is important information that must be reported.

steps.q: A manic client is making large impulsive purchases and giving money away. The technician recognizes this as:

opts.text: Impaired judgment from mania that calls for protective limits and reporting, not moral criticism
opts.rat: Impulsive, high-risk spending reflects manic impairment; the response is protective limit-setting and reporting, not judgment.

opts.text: A rational financial strategy the technician should encourage
opts.rat: Impulsive manic spending is not a sound strategy to encourage.

opts.text: Evidence the client is fully in control
opts.rat: This behavior reflects impaired judgment, not full control.

opts.text: A private matter that requires no attention
opts.rat: Risky manic behavior is a safety concern and is reported.

steps.q: When setting limits with a disruptive manic client, the technician should:

opts.text: Be calm, firm, brief, and consistent, and coordinate so all staff apply the same limits
opts.rat: Calm, consistent, unified limit-setting reduces manipulation and escalation and keeps expectations clear.

opts.text: Argue and debate at length to win the point
opts.rat: Lengthy arguing tends to escalate a manic client.

opts.text: Let each staff member set different rules
opts.rat: Inconsistent limits invite splitting and testing of boundaries.

opts.text: Use harsh punishment for every infraction
opts.rat: Punitive responses are nontherapeutic; consistent, respectful limits are used.

steps.q: A client's mania is subsiding and they now appear withdrawn, hopeless, and quietly tearful. The technician should be especially alert for:

opts.text: A shift into depression with possible suicide risk, and monitor safety and report
opts.rat: Bipolar clients can swing into depression as mania resolves; this raises suicide risk, so safety monitoring and reporting are essential.

opts.text: Nothing important, since the crisis is over
opts.rat: A swing into depression is a high-risk period, not a reason to relax vigilance.

opts.text: Only physical fatigue that needs no follow-up
opts.rat: The mood shift can carry suicide risk and requires monitoring.

opts.text: Certain full recovery requiring discharge today
opts.rat: A depressive shift is not a sign of recovery; it requires continued monitoring.

steps.q: A client with bipolar disorder wanting to become pregnant asks whether it is safe to keep taking her mood stabilizer. The technician should:

opts.text: Encourage her to discuss this with her provider, because some mood stabilizers carry risks in pregnancy and medication decisions belong to the prescriber
opts.rat: Certain mood stabilizers pose pregnancy risks; the technician refers the client to the provider rather than advising on the medication.

opts.text: Tell her to stop the medication immediately on her own
opts.rat: Advising an abrupt stop is outside scope and can destabilize the client.

opts.text: Assure her all psychiatric medications are completely safe in pregnancy
opts.rat: This is inaccurate and outside scope; the provider evaluates risks and options.

opts.text: Tell her the question does not matter
opts.rat: The question is important and is directed to the prescriber.

steps.q: Regarding the long-term monitoring a client on lithium needs (such as periodic kidney and thyroid checks), the technician's role is to:

opts.text: Support the client in keeping monitoring appointments and report symptoms, while ordering and interpreting labs belong to licensed staff
opts.rat: Lithium can affect the kidneys and thyroid over time; the technician encourages follow-up and reports symptoms, while ordering/interpreting labs is the licensed team's role.

opts.text: Order and interpret the client's kidney and thyroid labs independently
opts.rat: Ordering and interpreting labs is outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Tell the client long-term monitoring is unnecessary
opts.rat: Ongoing monitoring is important with long-term lithium.

opts.text: Adjust the lithium dose based on how the client looks
opts.rat: Dose adjustment is a prescriber decision, not the technician's.

steps.q: A manic client repeatedly interrupts and dominates a group activity. The BEST technician response is to:

opts.text: Calmly and respectfully redirect the client and reinforce group ground rules, offering a structured outlet for their energy
opts.rat: Respectful redirection and consistent ground rules manage the monopolizing behavior without shaming, and a structured outlet channels manic energy.

opts.text: Publicly criticize the client to make them stop
opts.rat: Public criticism is humiliating and can escalate the client.

opts.text: Remove the client from all activities indefinitely
opts.rat: Blanket exclusion is punitive; redirection and limits are tried first.

opts.text: Allow the client to dominate so the group stays calm
opts.rat: Allowing monopolizing undermines the group; gentle limits are set.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in caring for a manic client on lithium is to:

opts.text: Protect physical safety (rest, hydration, nutrition, impulse-related risk), watch for and report signs of lithium toxicity, reinforce consistent teaching and adherence, and report changes—while medical management belongs to licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician keeps the client physically safe, monitors for toxicity, supports adherence and teaching, and reports, while dosing and medical decisions are made by licensed staff.

opts.text: Independently adjust the client's lithium dose as needed
opts.rat: Adjusting the dose is outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Ignore signs of toxicity as long as the mood improves
opts.rat: Toxicity signs are recognized and reported regardless of mood.

opts.text: Judge the client for impulsive manic behavior
opts.rat: Care is nonjudgmental; behavior is managed with protective limits, not judgment.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Mental Health Care (bipolar/mania and mood-stabilizer safety) — Phase-2 depth/application. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level and stated conceptually, marked for faculty confirmation: acute-mania physical-safety priorities (exhaustion, dehydration, nutrition via portable finger foods, low-stimulation structured environment, impulse-related risk); lithium-toxicity recognition (coarse tremor, slurred speech, ataxia, vomiting, confusion) as an emergency requiring holding the dose and reporting; the situations that raise lithium levels (dehydration/fluid loss from vomiting-diarrhea, heat/exertion sweating, reduced sodium intake, NSAIDs, diuretics) applied as scenarios; sick-day and consistent fluid/salt teaching; the narrow therapeutic margin and the need for consistent dosing and ongoing lab monitoring; adherence and the pull of the manic 'high' handled nonjudgmentally; the depressive-swing/suicide-risk transition; referral of pregnancy medication questions to the prescriber; and the technician's monitoring/reporting/teaching-reinforcement role with dosing and lab interpretation reserved to licensed staff. Specific serum lithium numbers, exact reference ranges, and drug doses are NOT re-asserted here; the numeric lithium level and mood-stabilizer specifics are introduced in mh-core-03. Builds on and does not duplicate mh-core-03. Pending faculty review.
